title: THE TORAH FORBADE SEX WITH YOUR FATHER’S WIFE—Why Did Scripture Need to Say This?
paragraphs: THE TORAH FORBADE SEX WITH YOUR FATHER’S WIFE—Why Did Scripture Need to Say This?
One disturbing sentence in Leviticus exposes something terrifying about human desire—and something breathtaking about the God who refuses to leave sinners in darkness.
There are Bible verses we underline.
There are verses we frame.
There are verses we whisper over hospital beds and repeat when life is falling apart.
And then there are verses like this one.
You read it.
You stop.
You read it again.
And somewhere inside you, an uncomfortable question forms:
Why did God even have to say that?
Leviticus 18:8 reads:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא
‘Erwat eshet-avikha lo tegalleh; ‘erwat avikha hi.
Literally, the Hebrew says:
“The nakedness of your father’s wife you shall not uncover; it is your father’s nakedness.”
Not a comfortable sentence.
Not a verse likely to appear on a coffee mug.
But perhaps that discomfort is exactly why we need to hear it.
Because buried inside this prohibition is a devastating truth about humanity:
God gives commands in a world where human beings are capable of crossing boundaries we sometimes imagine nobody would ever cross.
And Scripture refuses to pretend otherwise.
That may be one reason Leviticus can feel so painfully modern.
It does not write about humanity as we wish humanity were.
It speaks into humanity as humanity actually is.
Broken.
Desiring.
Self-justifying.
Capable of tenderness one moment and betrayal the next.
Capable of protecting a family—and capable of destroying one.

Leviticus 18 does not emerge from a fantasy world populated by morally uncomplicated people. God was forming Israel as His covenant people among nations whose practices Israel was explicitly commanded not to imitate. The chapter repeatedly establishes boundaries around sexual relationships and family relationships.
And then comes verse 8.
Your father’s wife is forbidden to you.
Notice the wording carefully.
The Hebrew says אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ — eshet avikha: “your father’s wife.”

The wording matters because the previous verse has already addressed the nakedness of one’s father and mother. Verse 8 specifically addresses the wife of one’s father, naturally encompassing the situation of a stepmother or another woman occupying that marital relationship to the father.
Then comes the startling explanation:
עֶרְוַת אָבִיךָ הִוא — ‘erwat avikha hi.
“It is your father’s nakedness.”
In other words, sexual boundaries in Scripture are not merely about two bodies wanting something.
Relationships exist inside relationships.
Sex is never as isolated as sinful desire wants us to believe.
That is where this ancient command suddenly walks into the twenty-first century and sits beside us.
Because our culture loves one particular question:
“Do they both want it?”
Scripture asks deeper questions.
What covenant is being violated?
Whose trust is being betrayed?
What family is being wounded?
What boundary established by God is being crossed?
What does this desire do to another person?
And ultimately:
What does God say?
Sin has always tried to reduce morality to appetite.
“I want this.”
“I need this.”
“This makes me happy.”
“Nobody understands our relationship.”
“We love each other.”
“It’s complicated.”
But one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable revelations is that desire does not become holy simply because desire feels powerful.
You can desperately want something God has forbidden.
That sentence may hurt.
It may also save somebody.
Because some of the most destructive decisions of our lives begin when we quietly rename desire as destiny.
We feel something intensely, therefore we assume it must be authentic.
We experience attraction, therefore we assume pursuing it must be right.
We discover an opportunity, therefore we interpret the opportunity as permission.
But temptation often arrives carrying a counterfeit permission slip.
The existence of desire is not proof of divine approval.
And Leviticus 18 refuses to negotiate with desire when desire demands what belongs beyond God's boundary.
But here is where the passage becomes even more disturbing.
God apparently considered the warning necessary.
Think about that.
Why command people not to do something unless fallen human beings are capable of doing it?
The Bible understands us better than our carefully edited public lives suggest.
Scripture knows what human beings can become when desire is allowed to dethrone God.
And biblical history proves it.
Reuben went into Bilhah, his father Jacob’s concubine. Genesis records the act with painful brevity. Later, Jacob remembered it as the defiling of his bed.
Generations later, Absalom publicly went in to his father David’s concubines in an act loaded not merely with sexuality but humiliation, rebellion, and political domination.
Then we arrive in the New Testament.
And suddenly Leviticus 18:8 no longer feels ancient.
Paul writes to the church at Corinth that sexual immorality is being reported among them—specifically that a man has his father’s wife.
Read that again.
This wasn't happening in a pagan temple somewhere outside the church.
It was happening among people associated with the Christian community.
The scandal of Leviticus had walked straight into Corinth.
And perhaps the most frightening part of 1 Corinthians 5 is not merely that the sexual sin existed.
The church had apparently learned to coexist with it.
Paul expected grief.
Instead, there was pride.
That should frighten every generation of Christians.
Because there is something worse than falling into sin.
It is becoming comfortable enough with sin that repentance begins sounding offensive.
There is something worse than having darkness inside us.
It is redecorating the darkness and calling it freedom.
We rename lust “authenticity.”
We rename compromise “complexity.”
We rename cowardice “tolerance.”
We rename rebellion “being true to myself.”
And eventually we can become so skilled at changing vocabulary that we forget changing the name of a sin cannot change its nature before God.
Yet before you point toward somebody else’s scandal...
wait.
Because Leviticus 18 is holding a mirror, not handing you binoculars.
Maybe you have never touched your father’s wife.
Maybe the thought horrifies you.
But have you ever crossed a boundary you once swore you would never cross?
Have you ever deleted a conversation because you knew somebody should not see it?
Have you ever entertained an attraction you knew needed to die?
Have you ever kept returning mentally to something you knew dishonored Christ?
Have you ever called something “harmless” because admitting what it really was would require repentance?
Have you ever hidden behind “God knows my heart” while deliberately ignoring something God had already said?
Have you ever discovered that the person you thought you could never become was not as far away as you imagined?
That is where the self-righteous reader suddenly becomes quiet.
Because the Gospel does not divide humanity into scandalous sinners and respectable people.
It tells us that all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.
Different histories.
Different temptations.
Different consequences.
Different scars.
Same desperate need for a Savior.
And this is where we must be careful.
Grace does not mean God suddenly stops caring about holiness.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could make peace with the very sin from which He came to save us.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace is God doing something unimaginably costly about evil.
The cross proves simultaneously that our sin is worse than we wanted to admit...
and God's mercy is greater than we dared to hope.
Look at Jesus.
The One who never crossed the Father's boundary.
The One who never surrendered to temptation.
The One who never used another person's body for selfish gratification.
The One who never betrayed covenant faithfulness.
The One who remained perfectly obedient...
walked willingly toward a cross occupied by sinners.
There the Holy One was stripped.
Mocked.
Shamed.
Crucified.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the spotless Lamb of God.
And that changes the way we read Leviticus.
The commandments reveal God's holiness.
They expose human rebellion.
But the biblical story does not end with the sinner standing exposed.
It moves toward Christ.
Toward Calvary.
Toward an empty tomb.
Toward forgiveness offered to people whose stories cannot be cleaned up with public relations.
That includes sexual sinners.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The secretly addicted.
The ashamed.
The hypocrite who finally admits he has been pretending.
The woman carrying memories she cannot erase.
The man who wishes he could travel backward ten years and make one different decision.
The person reading this article while thinking:
“If people knew everything about me, they would never look at me the same way again.”
Jesus already knows.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
Not the Sunday version.
Everything.
And the Gospel invitation still stands:
Repent.
Come into the light.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Receive mercy.
This does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every wound we created, restore every relationship we shattered, or remove every responsibility created by our actions.
But in Jesus Christ, guilt does not have to become your eternal identity.
Your worst chapter does not have to become the title of your entire story.
That is the heartbeat behind these words:
Not because scandal was imaginary.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes people who were hiding and teaches them to walk in light.
He takes people enslaved by desire and teaches them obedience.
He takes people drowning in shame and clothes them in grace.
He takes people who spent years saying, “This is just who I am,” and begins transforming them into people who can finally say, “That is who I was—but Christ met me there.”
This is why biblical boundaries are not the enemy of love.
God does not establish sexual boundaries because He hates human flourishing.
The God who designed covenant, family, sexuality, faithfulness, and the human body knows what happens when desire consumes everything in its path.
A guardrail beside a cliff is not hatred.
Sometimes the boundary is there precisely because somebody knows how far the fall goes.
Maybe that is the answer to our original question.
Why did Scripture need to say this?
Because human beings need boundaries.
Because desire can become destructive.
Because families can be violated.
Because sin can persuade us to cross lines we once thought unthinkable.
Because God's people are not immune to scandal.
Because holiness must be taught.
Because repentance must remain possible.
And because God loves human beings enough to tell us no when our desires are leading us toward destruction.
But there is another reason this verse matters.
Someone reading this is not identifying with the sinner in the story.
You are identifying with the wounded family.
Somebody crossed a boundary against you.
Somebody else's appetite became your trauma.
Somebody who should have protected your home shattered it.
Maybe the scandal wasn't yours.
Maybe the scar was.
Hear this carefully:
What happened in your family does not place you beyond the reach of Christ's restoration.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend evil was good.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
Grace does not require rewriting evil as innocence.
Jesus can meet people inside histories they never chose.
He can restore what shame tried to steal.
He can teach the wounded that another person's sin does not have authority to define their worth.

And if this subject touches abuse, coercion, exploitation, or criminal behavior, spiritual language should never be used to silence victims or obstruct appropriate protection, reporting, accountability, or justice.
Biblical grace and truthful accountability are not enemies.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners also brings darkness into light.
So perhaps tonight the question is no longer:
“Why did God have to command something so obvious?”
Perhaps the question has become:
What boundary of God have I been slowly teaching myself to ignore?
That is a much harder question.
Don't answer publicly if doing so would expose private details or endanger you.
But answer God.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary.
No excuses.
Just truth.
“Jesus, this is where I have been hiding.”
That prayer may become the beginning of a completely different story.
Someone scrolling beneath you may desperately need to discover that Christians are not people without scars.
We are people learning where to bring them.
And please don't turn this article into ammunition for humiliating someone whose scandal is more visible than yours.
Not as a purchase of God's favor. Never.
Grace cannot be bought.
But one practical way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue is by willingly supporting the work and sharing biblical teaching with others.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
You cannot merchandise your way into holiness.
You cannot financially support enough Christian work to erase one sin.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Come to Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what darkness has been protecting.
Seek help where help is needed.
Make restitution where restitution is possible and appropriate.
Walk away from what Christ is calling you to leave.
And receive the grace you could never earn.
Because perhaps the most shocking thing about Leviticus 18 is not that human beings were capable of crossing horrifying boundaries.
We already know what humanity can do.
The greater wonder is that the God who knew exactly how deep human corruption could descend still chose to pursue sinners with redemption.
The Bible knows our scandals.
Calvary proves God did too.
And still...
Jesus came.
The boundary you crossed may explain the scar—but it does not have to write the ending when your story is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
